newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma City victims to view telecast of trial.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma City victims to view telecast of trial.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Wednesday chose a federal facility there for a closed-circuit telecast of the proceedings for victims of the blast because it can accomodate more people than a courtroom.

"We're going to make it work," U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch said at a short pre-trial hearing. A recently enacted law on terrorism provides for such a telecast when a trial has been moved to another city, as in the bombing trial.

Timothy McVeigh and his former army buddy Terry Nichols have been charged in the April 1995 bombing, which left 168 people dead and destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City. They face the death penalty.
Their cases have been separated. McVeigh's trial begins on March 31 and Nichols' at an undetermined later date.
The auditorium in a Federal Aviation Administration building, which can seat at least 300 people, would allow more victims to view the proceedings than federal courtrooms in Oklahoma City.

Marsha Kight, whose daugher Frankie Merrell was killed in the blast, told reporters the victims in Oklahoma City would be pleased that more seats will be available. She and several other people who lost relatives in the bombing have travelled to Denver to attend pre-trial hearings but for many such a trip is a hardship.
Matsch denied a request from news media in Oklahoma City to attend the closed-circuit telecast. He said the law provided for victims to view the telecast but not the media.
